claim: Hearing relies on rapid, temporally precise, and sustained neurotransmitter release at the ribbon synapses of inner hair cells (IHCs).
source: Hearing relies on rapid, temporally precise, and sustained neurotransmitter release at the ribbon synapses of sensory cells, the inner hair cells (IHCs).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the auditory system.

claim: Neurotransmitter release at IHC ribbon synapses requires otoferlin, a six C2-domain, Ca2+-binding transmembrane protein of synaptic vesicles.
source: This process requires otoferlin, a six C2-domain, Ca2+-binding transmembrane protein of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript and the experimental design of the study.

claim: Otof Ala515,Ala517/Ala515,Ala517 knock-in mice have lower Ca2+-binding affinity of the C2C domain.
source: To decipher the role of otoferlin in the synaptic vesicle cycle, we produced knock-in mice (Otof Ala515,Ala517/Ala515,Ala517) with lower Ca2+-binding affinity of the C2C domain.
evidence: This is the experimental design and prediction based on the mutations introduced.

claim: IHC ribbon synapse structure is unaffected in Otof C2C/C2C mutant mice.
source: The IHC ribbon synapse structure, synaptic Ca2+ currents, and otoferlin distribution were unaffected in these mutant mice
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Synaptic Ca2+ currents are unaffected in Otof C2C/C2C mutant mice.
source: The IHC ribbon synapse structure, synaptic Ca2+ currents, and otoferlin distribution were unaffected in these mutant mice
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5.

claim: Otoferlin distribution is unaffected in Otof C2C/C2C mutant mice.
source: The IHC ribbon synapse structure, synaptic Ca2+ currents, and otoferlin distribution were unaffected in these mutant mice
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Auditory brainstem response wave-I amplitude is reduced in Otof C2C/C2C mutant mice.
source: but auditory brainstem response wave-I amplitude was reduced
evidence: This is supported by ABR recordings shown in Figure 2.

claim: Lower Ca2+ sensitivity of the fast component of synaptic exocytosis is revealed in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs by membrane capacitance measurement.
source: Lower Ca2+ sensitivity and delay of the fast and sustained components of synaptic exocytosis were revealed by membrane capacitance measurement upon modulations of intracellular Ca2+ concentration
evidence: This is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Delay of the fast component of synaptic exocytosis is revealed in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs by membrane capacitance measurement.
source: Lower Ca2+ sensitivity and delay of the fast and sustained components of synaptic exocytosis were revealed by membrane capacitance measurement upon modulations of intracellular Ca2+ concentration
evidence: This is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Lower Ca2+ sensitivity of the sustained component of synaptic exocytosis is revealed in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs by membrane capacitance measurement.
source: Lower Ca2+ sensitivity and delay of the fast and sustained components of synaptic exocytosis were revealed by membrane capacitance measurement upon modulations of intracellular Ca2+ concentration
evidence: This is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 8.

claim: Delay of the sustained component of synaptic exocytosis is revealed in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs by membrane capacitance measurement.
source: Lower Ca2+ sensitivity and delay of the fast and sustained components of synaptic exocytosis were revealed by membrane capacitance measurement upon modulations of intracellular Ca2+ concentration
evidence: This is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 8.

claim: Otoferlin functions as a Ca2+ sensor for primed vesicle fusion with the presynaptic plasma membrane in IHCs.
source: Otoferlin thus functions as a Ca2+ sensor, setting the rates of primed vesicle fusion with the presynaptic plasma membrane and synaptic vesicle pool replenishment in the IHC active zone.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Otoferlin functions as a Ca2+ sensor for synaptic vesicle pool replenishment in the IHC active zone.
source: Otoferlin thus functions as a Ca2+ sensor, setting the rates of primed vesicle fusion with the presynaptic plasma membrane and synaptic vesicle pool replenishment in the IHC active zone.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Sound-evoked mechanical stimulation of the IHC hair bundle induces changes in membrane potential that modulate synaptic exocytosis with submillisecond precision.
source: Sound-evoked mechanical stimulation of the IHC sensory antenna, the hair bundle, induces changes in membrane potential, modulating synaptic exocytosis with submillisecond precision (Glowatzki and Fuchs, 2002; Goutman, 2012; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The temporal precision of IHC synaptic exocytosis exceeds that for most conventional synapses.
source: This temporal precision exceeds that for most conventional synapses
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Sound-evoked action potentials of primary auditory neurons can be phase-locked to sinusoidal acoustic signals up to frequencies of ~4 kHz.
source: and allows sound-evoked action potentials of the primary auditory neurons to be phase-locked to the sinusoidal acoustic signal up to frequencies of ~4 kHz (Fuchs, 2005; Moser et al., 2006; Safieddine et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: IHCs can maintain neurotransmitter release at high frequency for several minutes.
source: In addition, IHCs can maintain neurotransmitter release at high frequency for several minutes (Kiang, 1965)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The basolateral region of IHCs contains 10 to 30 synaptic active zones.
source: The basolateral region of IHCs contains 10 to 30 synaptic active zones
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about IHCs.

claim: Each IHC synaptic active zone faces the single dendritic bouton of a primary auditory neuron.
source: each of which faces the single dendritic bouton of a primary auditory neuron
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about IHC synapses.

claim: Most vesicles in each IHC synapse are tethered to a ribbon-shaped osmiophilic structure.
source: Most of the vesicles in each synapse are tethered to a ribbon-shaped osmiophilic structure (hence the name 'ribbon synapse')
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about ribbon synapses.

claim: Ribbon-tethered vesicles presumably form a pool of primed vesicles for immediate and sustained replenishment of the fusion-competent vesicle pool.
source: presumably forming a pool of primed vesicles for the immediate and sustained replenishment of the pool of fusion-competent vesicles located between the base of the ribbon and the presynaptic plasma membrane (von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1997; Lenzi et al., 1999; Moser and Beutner, 2000).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mature IHCs lack several common synaptic proteins.
source: Mature IHCs lack several common synaptic proteins (Safieddine and Wenthold, 1999; Vogl et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mature IHC synapses lack synaptotagmin 1 and synaptotagmin 2.
source: In particular, mature IHC synapses lack the synaptic vesicle transmembrane proteins synaptotagmin 1 and 2 (Syt1 and Syt2) (Safieddine and Wenthold, 1999; Beurg et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Synaptotagmin 1 and 2 function as Ca2+ sensors for rapid, synchronous neurotransmitter release at central nervous system synapses.
source: which function as Ca2+ sensors for rapid, synchronous neurotransmitter release at central nervous system synapses (Südhof, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Synaptotagmin proteins contain two cytoplasmic C2-domains that bind to membrane phospholipids in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: These proteins, which contain two cytoplasmic C2-domains, bind to membrane phospholipids in a Ca2+-dependent manner (Brose et al., 1992; Sutton et al., 1995; Wang et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Synaptotagmins trigger the final steps of synaptic exocytosis by interacting with complexin and the SNARE molecular complex.
source: and trigger the final steps of synaptic exocytosis by interacting with complexin and the SNARE molecular complex (Bennett et al., 1992; Söllner et al., 1993; Li et al., 1995; Giraudo et al., 2006; Südhof, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: IHC vesicles contain otoferlin, a Ca2+-binding single-pass membrane protein with six C2 domains and two Fer domains.
source: However, unlike vesicles of central nervous system synapses, IHC vesicles contain otoferlin, a Ca2+-binding single-pass membrane protein with six C2 domains (C2A-F) and two Fer domains in its cytoplasmic region (Yasunaga et al., 1999; Roux et al., 2006; Lek et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Otoferlin belongs to the ferlin family, which is thought to have originated earlier than synaptotagmins and E-synaptotagmins during evolution.
source: Otoferlin belongs to the ferlin family, which is thought to have originated earlier than synaptotagmins and E-synaptotagmins during evolution (Lek et al., 2012) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Otoferlin is defective in a recessive form of profound congenital deafness.
source: Otoferlin, defective in a recessive form of profound congenital deafness (Yasunaga et al., 1999; Roux et al., 2006; Lek et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Otoferlin is required for normal synaptic exocytosis in auditory hair cells.
source: is required for normal synaptic exocytosis in auditory (Roux et al., 2006) and vestibular hair cells (Dulon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Otoferlin is required for normal synaptic exocytosis in vestibular hair cells.
source: is required for normal synaptic exocytosis in auditory (Roux et al., 2006) and vestibular hair cells (Dulon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: IHC synaptic exocytosis is almost entirely abolished in adult Otof -/- mice.
source: IHC synaptic exocytosis is almost entirely abolished in adult mutant mice lacking otoferlin (Otof -/- mice), despite normal Ca2+ currents and ribbon synapse morphogenesis (Roux et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Ca2+ currents are normal in adult Otof -/- mice.
source: IHC synaptic exocytosis is almost entirely abolished in adult mutant mice lacking otoferlin (Otof -/- mice), despite normal Ca2+ currents and ribbon synapse morphogenesis (Roux et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Ribbon synapse morphogenesis is normal in adult Otof -/- mice.
source: IHC synaptic exocytosis is almost entirely abolished in adult mutant mice lacking otoferlin (Otof -/- mice), despite normal Ca2+ currents and ribbon synapse morphogenesis (Roux et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: It has been hypothesized that otoferlin acts as the major Ca2+ sensor triggering synaptic vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane in the IHC active zone.
source: This finding, together with the absence of Syt1, Syt2, and Syt9 from mature IHCs (Safieddine and Wenthold, 1999; Beurg et al., 2010), has led to the hypothesis that otoferlin acts as the major Ca2+ sensor triggering synaptic vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane in the IHC active zone (Roux et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior research findings.

claim: The Pachanga mutant mouse harbors a missense mutation in the otoferlin C2F domain.
source: The Pachanga mutant, a deaf mouse harboring a missense mutation in the otoferlin C2F domain, showed unaffected vesicle fusion but a major decrease of the sustained component of IHC synaptic exocytosis (Pangrsic et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The Pachanga mutant showed unaffected vesicle fusion but a major decrease of the sustained component of IHC synaptic exocytosis.
source: The Pachanga mutant, a deaf mouse harboring a missense mutation in the otoferlin C2F domain, showed unaffected vesicle fusion but a major decrease of the sustained component of IHC synaptic exocytosis (Pangrsic et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Pangrsic and colleagues suggested a role for otoferlin in synaptic vesicle pool replenishment based on the Pachanga mutant phenotype.
source: which led Pangrsic and coll. to suggest a role for otoferlin in synaptic vesicle pool replenishment.

claim: The Pachanga mutation does not target a Ca2+-binding site.
source: However, the Ca2+ sensing role of otoferlin could not be assessed in the Pachanga mice because the mutation does not target a Ca2+-binding site and the otoferlin cell content is much lower than normal.

claim: Otoferlin cell content is much lower than normal in Pachanga mice.
source: However, the Ca2+ sensing role of otoferlin could not be assessed in the Pachanga mice because the mutation does not target a Ca2+-binding site and the otoferlin cell content is much lower than normal.

source: Of note, Otof I515T/I515T knock-in mice, harboring a Ile515Thr missense mutation in the C2C domain, also display abnormal synaptic exocytosis and sustained release (Strenzke et al., 2016).

claim: Otof I515T/I515T knock-in mice display abnormal synaptic exocytosis and sustained release.
source: Of note, Otof I515T/I515T knock-in mice, harboring a Ile515Thr missense mutation in the C2C domain, also display abnormal synaptic exocytosis and sustained release (Strenzke et al., 2016).

claim: The Ile515Thr mutation results in a strongly reduced otoferlin content.
source: Similarly to the Pachanga mutation, the Ile515Thr mutation does not affect the Ca2+-binding site of the C2 domain, and results in a strongly reduced otoferlin content

claim: Ten candidate models of the otoferlin C2C domain were calculated with MODELLER based on the X-ray structure of human dysferlin C2A domain.
source: Ten candidate models were calculated with MODELLER (Webb and Sali, 2014), based on the X-ray structure of the human dysferlin C2A domain (4ihb) (Fuson et al., 2014).

claim: The primary sequence identity between dysferlin C2A and mouse otoferlin C2C is 23%.

claim: ABR thresholds were similar in Otof +/+ and Otof C2C/+ mice at one month of age.
source: At the age of one month, ABR thresholds were similar in Otof +/+ (n = 5) and Otof C2C/+ (n = 4) mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, p>0.3)
evidence: This is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ABR thresholds were slightly higher in Otof C2C/C2C mice than in Otof C2C/+ mice at one month of age.
source: but they were slightly higher in Otof C2C/C2C mice (n = 11), by about 5.4 ± 3.3 dB, on average, than in Otof C2C/+ mice (n = 9), for all frequencies tested (Figure 2A; two-way-ANOVA, p=0.04)
evidence: This is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The mean peak amplitude for ABR wave-I was lower in Otof C2C/C2C mice than in Otof C2C/+ mice by a factor of 2.7 at one month of age.
source: The mean peak amplitude for ABR wave-I (in response to 100–200 tone bursts), reflecting the synchronous electrical response of primary afferent neurons, was lower in Otof C2C⁄C2Cmice (n = 7) than in Otof C2C/+ mice (n = 7), by a factor of 2.7 (Figure 2B–C and E) (p=0.006).
evidence: This is supported by ABR data shown in Figures 2B, 2C, and 2E.

claim: The lower ABR wave-I amplitude in Otof C2C/C2C mice did not affect ABR waves-II to V.
source: This lower ABR wave-I amplitude did not affect ABR waves-II to V, which reflect the mean neuronal activity of the cochlear nucleus and higher auditory relays (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ABR thresholds of Otof C2C/C2C mice were similar to those of Otof C2C/+ mice on postnatal days 16-21.

evidence: This is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ABR wave-I amplitude was already lower in Otof C2C/C2C mice than in Otof C2C/+ mice on postnatal days 16-21.

evidence: This is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ABR thresholds increased in Otof C2C/C2C mice from the age of three months onwards.

evidence: This is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The peak amplitude of ABR wave-I decreased further by a factor of about 10 in Otof C2C/C2C mice from three months onwards.
source: The peak amplitude of the ABR wave-I also decreased further by a factor of about 10 (p<0.01, for all ages, with a minimum of 5 animals per group; Figure 2E).

claim: Distortion-product otoacoustic emissions were similar in Otof C2C/+ and Otof C2C/C2C mice.

claim: Cochlear amplification of sound stimuli was preserved in Otof C2C/C2C mice.

claim: The auditory phenotype of Otof C2C/C2C mice is consistent with the restriction of otoferlin dysfunction to IHCs.

evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5A2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The corresponding ΔCm also peaked at about −10 mV.
source: The corresponding ΔCm also peaked at about −10 mV (Figure 5A2, bottom and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5A2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The evoked ΔCm was identical in Otof +/+ and Otof C2C/+ IHCs.
source: In Otof +/+ and Otof C2C/+ IHCs, the evoked ΔCm was identical (two-way-ANOVA, p=0.93; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, bottom)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: For depolarization to −30 mV and beyond, ΔCm was significantly smaller in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs.
source: However, for depolarization to −30 mV and beyond (see dashed line in Figure 5A2), corresponding to a high open probability of Ca2+-channels and a decreasing driving force for Ca2+ entry, ΔCm was significantly smaller in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (two-way-ANOVA, p<10−4).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5A2.

claim: A 1.6-fold decrease in ΔCm was observed for depolarization to −10 mV between Otof C2C/+ and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs.
source: A 1.6-fold decrease was observed for depolarization to −10 mV.
evidence: This is a quantification of the electrophysiological data.

claim: The Ca2+ efficiency of RRP release was lower (by a factor of 1.7) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs.
source: The Ca2+ efficiency of RRP release, evaluated by plotting the mean derivative of ΔCm against ICa, was lower (by a factor of 1.7) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs ((3.9 ± 0.7) x 10−2 fF.pA−1) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs ((6.6 ± 0.4) x 10−2 fF.pA−1) (Figure 5A3; 95% confidence interval of the fitted slope).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5A3.

claim: For depolarizations of 2 and 5 ms, the ΔCm values in Otof C2C/C2C mice were about a third and a half those in Otof C2C/+ mice, respectively.
source: For depolarizations of 2 and 5 ms, the ΔCm values in Otof C2C/C2C mice (n = 16) were about a third (p=0.01) and a half (p=0.02) those in Otof C2C/+ mice (n = 11), respectively
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5B2.

claim: The slope of the ΔCm versus depolarization duration fit was lower (by a factor of 1.5) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (0.46 ± 0.04 fF.ms−1) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (0.69 ± 0.05 fF.ms−1).
source: By fitting the average relationship between ΔCm and depolarization duration (Δt) for the shortest depolarizations, we found that the slope of this fit, taken as an approximation of the Ca2+ sensitivity of release, was lower (by a factor of 1.5) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (0.46 ± 0.04 fF.ms−1) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (0.69 ± 0.05 fF.ms−1) (Figure 5B2; 95% confidence interval of the fitted slope).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5B2.

claim: In Otof C2C/+ IHCs, RRP release at intracellular EGTA concentrations of 0.5 mM and 5 mM was similar for depolarization durations between 2 and 10 ms.
source: In Otof C2C/+ IHCs, RRP release at intracellular EGTA concentrations of 0.5 mM (n = 11) and 5 mM (n = 9) was similar for depolarization durations between 2 and 10 ms, reflecting a tight coupling of Ca2+ channels to RRP vesicles (Figure 5B3, top, two-way-ANOVA, p=0.3 for the 2–10 ms interval and p=3×10−4 for the 2–30 ms interval).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5B3.

claim: In Otof C2C/C2C IHCs, RRP release at intracellular EGTA concentrations of 0.5 mM and 5 mM was similar for depolarization durations between 2 and 10 ms.
source: In Otof C2C/C2C IHCs, RRP release at intracellular EGTA concentrations of 0.5 mM (n = 16) and 5 mM (n = 10) was also similar for depolarization durations between 2 and 10 ms (Figure 5B3, bottom; two-way-ANOVA, p=0.2 for the 2–30 ms interval)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5B3.

claim: The spatial coupling between voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and RRP vesicles is not modified by the otoferlin C2C domain mutations.
source: suggesting that the spatial coupling between voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and RRP vesicles is not modified by the otoferlin C2C domain mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EGTA experiments.

claim: The exocytotic response of Otof C2C/C2C IHCs rapidly saturated for depolarizations lasting 15–20 ms.
source: Remarkably, unlike the exocytotic response of Otof C2C/+ IHCs, which did not plateau for depolarizations lasting up to 50 ms, that of Otof C2C/C2C IHCs rapidly saturated for depolarizations lasting 15–20 ms (Figure 5B2)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5B2.

claim: Vesicle pool replenishment at the release sites was impaired in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs.
source: and was insensitive to 5 mM intracellular EGTA (Figure 5B3), suggesting that vesicle pool replenishment at the release sites was also impaired in these cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data shown in Figures 5B2 and 5B3.

claim: For any given level of Ca2+ current, synaptic release in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs was only about half that in Otof C2C/+ IHCs.
source: However, for any given level of Ca2+ current, synaptic release in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs was only about half that in Otof C2C/+ IHCs.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5C2.

claim: The Ca2+ sensitivity of release was lower (by a factor of 2.2) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs when varying extracellular Ca2+ concentration.
source: Moreover, the Ca2+ sensitivity of release, evaluated by fitting a linear function to the ΔCm/ICa curve, was lower (by a factor of 2.2) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs ((2.2 ± 0.5) x 10−2 fF.pA−1) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs ((4.8 ± 1.0) x 10−2 fF.pA−1) (Figure 5C2; 95% confidence interval of the fitted slope).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5C2.

claim: C2C domain mutations decrease the Ca2+-dependent efficiency and kinetics of RRP vesicle fusion.
source: Together, these results support the notion that C2C domain mutations decrease the Ca2+-dependent efficiency and kinetics of RRP vesicle fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data.

claim: Total synaptic release upon Ca2+ uncaging was similar in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (2.25 ± 0.18 pF) and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (2.19 ± 0.22 pF).
source: This protocol, which triggered a rapid and global increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration, from a few tens of nM to up to 59 ± 7 µM (n = 7) (Vincent et al., 2015), led to a total synaptic release that was similar in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (2.25 ± 0.18 pF; n = 18) and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (2.19 ± 0.22 pF; n = 19; Mann-Whitney test, p=0.4; Figure 6A)
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ uncaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: All vesicles in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs can fuse when exposed to high Ca2+ concentrations throughout the entire vesicle cycle pathway.
source: This result suggests that all the vesicles in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs can fuse when exposed to high Ca2+ concentrations throughout the entire vesicle cycle pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Ca2+ uncaging data.

claim: The onset of synaptic release was delayed in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (7.3 ± 1.2 ms) compared to Otof C2C/+ IHCs (4.2 ± 0.7 ms) upon Ca2+ uncaging.
source: The most striking features were the delayed onset of synaptic release and the longer time required to reach the maximal rate of release in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (7.3 ± 1.2 ms and 52.1 ± 9.2 ms, respectively) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (4.2 ± 0.7 ms and 24.3 ± 2.7 ms, respectively; Mann-Whitney test, p=0.02 and p=0.001, respectively; Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ uncaging data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: The time required to reach the maximal rate of release was longer in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (52.1 ± 9.2 ms) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (24.3 ± 2.7 ms) upon Ca2+ uncaging.
source: The most striking features were the delayed onset of synaptic release and the longer time required to reach the maximal rate of release in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (7.3 ± 1.2 ms and 52.1 ± 9.2 ms, respectively) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (4.2 ± 0.7 ms and 24.3 ± 2.7 ms, respectively; Mann-Whitney test, p=0.02 and p=0.001, respectively; Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ uncaging data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: The maximal rate of release was lower (by a factor of 1.6) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (67 ± 14 fF.ms−1) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (107 ± 23 fF.ms−1) upon Ca2+ uncaging.
source: The maximal rate of release was also lower (by a factor of 1.6) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (67 ± 14 fF.ms−1, corresponding to 1490 ± 310 vesicles/ms) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (107 ± 23 fF.ms−1, corresponding to 2380 ± 510 vesicles/ms; Mann-Whitney test, p=0.03; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ uncaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The kinetics of the intracellular Ca2+ increase in Otof C2C/+ and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs upon UV flash were similar.
source: In these recording conditions, the kinetics of the intracellular Ca2+ increase in Otof C2C/+ (t = 28.8 ± 1.7 ms; n = 6) and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (26.6 ± 9.2 ms; n = 7) upon UV flash were similar (p=0.8)
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: No major effect on the cooperativity of release was detected in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (Hill coefficient value: 3.3 ± 0.3 for both genotypes).
source: No major effect on the cooperativity of release was detected in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (Hill coefficient value: 3.3 ± 0.3 for both genotypes; p>0.9; Figure 7B)
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ uncaging and imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The Ca2+ sensitivity of vesicle fusion was about four times lower in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (EC50: 9.8 ± 0.7 µM) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (EC50: 2.3 ± 0.6 µM).
source: whereas the Ca2+ sensitivity of vesicle fusion was about four times lower in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (EC50: 9.8 ± 0.7 µM) than that in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (EC50: 2.3 ± 0.6 µM; p=0.004; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ uncaging and imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The Ca2+ uncaging results are consistent with a deleterious effect of C2C domain mutations on the Ca2+ affinity of otoferlin for triggering and setting the rate of RRP vesicle fusion.
source: Taking into account the normal number of docked vesicles in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (Figure 4) and the lower efficiency of Ca2+-dependent exocytosis following the activation of their Ca2+ channels (Figure 5 C1–C2), these Ca2+ uncaging results are consistent with a deleterious effect of C2C domain mutations on the Ca2+ affinity of otoferlin for triggering and setting the rate of RRP vesicle fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Ca2+ uncaging and structural data.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio of release was much lower (by a factor of 2.2 at its minimum value) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs for interpulse intervals of up to 500 ms.
source: The paired-pulse ratio of release, used as a proxy for RRP replenishment, was much lower (by a factor of 2.2 at its minimum value) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (n = 13) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (n = 9), for interpulse intervals of up to 500 ms (two-way ANOVA, p<10−4).
evidence: This is supported by paired-pulse electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The impairment of sustained release in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs is not merely a consequence of impaired RRP release; the recruitment of synaptic vesicles per se is also defective.
source: This result led us to conclude that the impairment of sustained release in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs is not merely a consequence of impaired RRP release; the recruitment of synaptic vesicles per se is also defective.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the paired-pulse data.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio recovered fully at interpulse intervals of about 1 s.
source: However, the paired-pulse ratio recovered fully at interpulse intervals of about 1 s.
evidence: This is supported by paired-pulse electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The rate of exocytosis in response to long depolarizations was much lower (by a factor of 5.3) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (80 fF/s) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (420 fF/s).
source: We probed the response of Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (n = 8) to long depolarizations to −10 mV of up to 3 s and observed a much lower (by a factor of 5.3) rate of exocytosis than that measured in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (n = 8; 80 fF/s versus 420 fF/s; two-way ANOVA, p<10−4; Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Periodic stimulation with 50 short depolarizations induced a mean ΔCm of 51 fF in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs.
source: This periodic stimulation induced a mean ΔCm of 51 fF in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The rate of vesicle pool replenishment is about 1.5 vesicles/ms/IHC in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs.
source: Assuming full depletion of the RRP by the train of depolarizations, we can estimate the rate of vesicle pool replenishment at about 1.5 vesicles/ms/IHC in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs, a much lower value (by a factor of 3.7) than obtained for Otof C2C/+ IHCs (~5.6 vesicles/ms/IHC).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: The linear replenishment component was less efficient (by a factor of 2.8) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (0.6 fF per depolarization step) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (1.7 fF per depolarization step).
source: The linear replenishment component was less efficient (by a factor of 2.8) in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (n = 17) than in Otof C2C/+ IHCs (n = 12), at 0.6 fF and 1.7 fF per depolarization step, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Superlinear release was observed in only one of seventeen Otof C2C/C2C IHCs subjected to trains of depolarization.
source: In Otof C2C/C2C IHCs, superlinear release was observed in only one of seventeen Otof C2C/C2C IHCs subjected to such trains of depolarization, whereas it was observed in six of the twelve Otof C2C/+ IHCs studied and six of the eleven Otof  +/+ IHCs studied (Fisher's exact test, p=0.01).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: The almost total absence of superlinear release in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs was probably unlinked to intracellular Ca2+ diffusion defects.
source: This almost total absence of superlinear release in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs was probably unlinked to intracellular Ca2+ diffusion defects, because the patterns of calcium entry and diffusion imaged by high-speed swept-field confocal microscopy in IHCs loaded with OGB-5N were similar in Otof C2C/+ (n = 10–12) and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (n = 6–10).
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C2C domain mutations did not affect the temporal and spatial dynamics of Ca2+ entry and diffusion around the synaptic ribbon.
source: Thus, the C2C domain mutations did not affect the temporal and spatial dynamics of Ca2+ entry and diffusion around the synaptic ribbon (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Otoferlin may function as the Ca2+ sensor triggering superlinear release.
source: These results suggest that otoferlin may also function as the Ca2+ sensor triggering superlinear release.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological and Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: Both slow and fast modes of membrane retrieval following IHC depolarization were observed in Otof C2C/+ and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs.
source: In Otof C2C/+ and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs, both these modes of endocytosis were observed (Figure 9A–B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 9A, 9B, and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: A 100 ms depolarization was sufficient to observe the exponential component of endocytosis in seven of the eight Otof C2C/+ IHCs studied.
source: However, a 100 ms depolarization was sufficient to observe the exponential component of endocytosis in seven of the eight Otof C2C/+ IHCs studied, but the same protocol elicited the exponential component in only one of the 10 Otof C2C/C2C IHCs recorded (Fisher's exact test, p=0.003).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: The rate of the slow component of endocytosis was similar in Otof C2C/+ (6.4 ± 0.8 fF.s−1) and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (5.3 ± 0.5 fF.s−1).
source: In IHCs for which values of 20 to 150 fF had previously been recorded for exocytosis, the rate of the slow component was similar in Otof C2C/+ (6.4 ± 0.8 fF.s−1, n = 8) and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (5.3 ± 0.5 fF.s−1, n = 9; p=0.24; Figure 9A)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The time constant and amplitude of the exponential component of endocytosis were similar in Otof C2C/+ and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs.
source: Likewise, when considering IHCs with an amplitude of the exponential component of endocytosis exceeding 100 fF, the time constant and amplitude of the exponential component of endocytosis were similar in Otof C2C/+ (3.2 ± 0.5 s and 266 ± 44 fF, respectively, n = 8) and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (3.4 ± 0.3 s and 244 ± 34 fF, respectively, n = 6; p>0.7 for both comparisons; Figure 9B)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Endocytosis kinetics following Ca2+ uncaging were similar in Otof C2C/+ and Otof C2C/C2C IHCs.
source: In these experimental conditions, endocytosis kinetics were also similar in Otof C2C/+ (n = 13) and Otof C2C/C2C (n = 15; p=0.17; Figure 9C) IHCs.
evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ uncaging data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Endocytosis is unaffected in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs.
source: Together, our results indicate that endocytosis is unaffected in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the endocytosis data.

claim: Mean EPSC amplitude did not differ significantly between Otof C2C/C2C and Otof +/+ IHCs.
source: Mean EPSC amplitude and EPSC decay time constant did not differ significantly between Otof C2C/C2C (n = 8) and Otof +/+ IHCs (n = 8; p>0.3; Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by postsynaptic EPSC recording data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: EPSC decay time constant did not differ significantly between Otof C2C/C2C and Otof +/+ IHCs.
source: Mean EPSC amplitude and EPSC decay time constant did not differ significantly between Otof C2C/C2C (n = 8) and Otof +/+ IHCs (n = 8; p>0.3; Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by postsynaptic EPSC recording data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The mean EPSC rate in the first 10 s following 25 mM KCl application was slower in Otof C2C/C2C than in Otof +/+ IHCs (by a factor of 3.3).
source: The mean EPSC rate in the first 10 s following 25 mM KCl application was, however, slower in Otof C2C/C2C than in Otof +/+ IHCs (by a factor of 3.3; Figure 10C, p=0.003)
evidence: This is supported by postsynaptic EPSC recording data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Single-vesicle and multivesicular release events were observed in both Otof C2C/C2C and Otof +/+ IHCs.
source: Single-vesicle and multivesicular release events were observed in both Otof C2C/C2C and Otof +/+ IHCs (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by postsynaptic EPSC recording data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The distribution of EPSC amplitudes was more variable in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs than in Otof +/+ IHCs.
source: However, the distribution of EPSC amplitudes was more variable in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs than in Otof +/+ IHCs (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<10−3; Figure 10D)
evidence: This is supported by postsynaptic EPSC recording data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: The results do not support the existence of a specific effect of the C2C domain mutations on one release mechanism (uniquantal or multiquantal) rather than the other.
source: Our results do not support the existence of a specific effect of the C2C domain mutations on one release mechanism — uniquantal (Chapochnikov et al., 2014) or multiquantal (Li et al., 2014) — rather than the other.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the postsynaptic EPSC recording data.

claim: The synaptic vesicles of Otof C2C/C2C IHCs can fuse with the plasma membrane, but at a slower rate than those of Otof +/+ IHCs.
source: Overall, our postsynaptic EPSC recordings confirmed that the synaptic vesicles of Otof C2C/C2C IHCs can fuse with the plasma membrane, but at a slower rate than those of Otof +/+ IHCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the postsynaptic EPSC recording data.

claim: Changes in the K1, K2, and K3 transition rates were sufficient to reproduce the main features of the impairment of synaptic exocytosis observed in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs.
source: Changes in the K1, K2, and K3 transition rates were, therefore, sufficient to reproduce the main features of the impairment of synaptic exocytosis observed in Otof C2C/C2C IHCs (slower RRP depletion, lower rate of linear release, and absence of superlinear release) (Figure 11C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figures 11C and 11D.

claim: The same Ca2+ sensor, otoferlin, is involved in synaptic vesicle fusion and in synaptic vesicle pool replenishment at the IHC ribbon synapse.
source: We show here that the same Ca2+ sensor, otoferlin, is involved in synaptic vesicle fusion and in synaptic vesicle pool replenishment at the IHC ribbon synapse.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, drawn from all the experimental data.

claim: In many synapses, different steps of the synaptic vesicle cycle involve different Ca2+ sensors.
source: In many synapses, different steps of the synaptic vesicle cycle involve different Ca2+ sensors.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: At the calyx of Held synapse, Syt2 drives synchronous vesicular exocytosis.
source: For instance, at the calyx of Held synapse, Syt2 drives synchronous vesicular exocytosis (Sun et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: At the calyx of Held synapse, vesicle pool replenishment requires the Ca2+-calmodulin-Munc13-1 complex.
source: and vesicle pool replenishment requires the Ca2+-calmodulin-Munc13-1 complex (Lipstein et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: At hippocampal synapses, rapid vesicular exocytosis depends on Syt1.
source: Likewise, rapid vesicular exocytosis at hippocampal synapses depends on Syt1
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: At hippocampal synapses, vesicle pool replenishment involves Syt7 and calmodulin.
source: whereas vesicle pool replenishment involves Syt7 and calmodulin (Liu et al., 2014; Jackman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: At the neuromuscular junction in drosophila, Syt1 is involved both in exocytosis and endocytosis.
source: At the neuromuscular junction in drosophila, Syt1 is involved both in exocytosis and endocytosis (Poskanzer et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In mouse cerebellum basket cells, Syt2 mediates fast vesicle pool replenishment.
source: and in mouse cerebellum basket cells, the major Ca2+ sensor for exocytosis, Syt2, also mediates fast vesicle pool replenishment (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mature IHC ribbon synapses lack several proteins critical for vesicle fusion in synapses of the central nervous system, including Syt1, Syt2, complexins, synaptophysin, and Munc13.
source: Mature IHC ribbon synapses lack several proteins critical for vesicle fusion in synapses of the central nervous system, including Syt1 and Syt2 (Safieddine and Wenthold, 1999; Beurg et al., 2010), complexins, which act as important regulators of spontaneous and fast synchronous Ca2+-evoked fusion (Giraudo et al., 2006; Strenzke et al., 2009; Krishnakumar et al., 2011; Lai et al., 2014), synaptophysin (Safieddine and Wenthold, 1999), and Munc13 (Vogl et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neuronal SNARE proteins have been reported to be dispensable for exocytosis at the IHC ribbon synapse.
source: In addition, neuronal SNARE proteins (synaptobrevins, snap-25, and syntaxin-1) have been reported to be dispensable for exocytosis at the IHC ribbon synapse, suggesting that other molecular components take on the role of these proteins (Nouvian et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The singular molecular setting of the mature IHC ribbon synapse presumably optimizes the coordination between fast vesicle fusion and synaptic vesicle pool replenishment.
source: Such a singular molecular setting of the mature IHC ribbon synapse presumably optimizes the coordination between fast vesicle fusion and synaptic vesicle pool replenishment, allowing this synapse to operate indefatigably at high rates and with a high degree of temporal precision.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings of the study.
